title: Community helpers and shared things: how a neighbourhood keeps going

summary.text: A neighbourhood runs on the work of many people: the milk delivery person, the sweeper, the postwoman, the nurse and the shopkeeper. It also runs on things that many people share, such as a water tank, a lift, a park or a pond. In this unit you list the helpers who keep your building going, and find out what public services like schools, health centres, the post office and the municipality do. Then you play a real test with a pond of chana fish, once in silence and once after agreeing a rule. You find out why some shared things run out and others last for hundreds of years.
summary.art: An Indian apartment building seen from the street in the morning, with a milk delivery person, a woman sweeping, a postwoman with a bag and a water lorry at the gate, and a shared water tank on the roof.

intro.hook: Twelve families share one water tank. Nobody owns it alone. Why does it sometimes run dry by afternoon, even on a day the lorry came?
intro.text: A community is a group of people who live near each other and depend on each other. Some of them do work for everyone: they bring milk, sweep the road, teach, nurse and deliver letters. Some things belong to everyone together, like a tank, a lift or a park. A shared thing can be used up when each person takes what they want. In this unit you test what keeps a shared thing going, with a bowl of chana and your own family.
intro.art: A girl on the terrace of a flat looking into an open water tank, with water tank pipes going down the side of the building.

outcomes: I can name helpers in my neighbourhood, say what each one does, and explain how my family depends on them.
I can explain why every job needs skill and deserves respect, and that in India every person may choose their work.

I can say what public services such as a government school, a health centre, the post office, the water supply, garbage collection, the police and the fire service do, who pays for them, and when to call 112.
I can explain what a shared resource is, and give examples from my building, my street and my city.
I can run the Shared Pond Test, write the results in a table, and use my evidence to explain why the pond lasted or ran out.
I can tell how Elinor Ostrom showed that many communities look after shared things with rules they make themselves.
I can suggest a fair rule for a shared thing, and say how people would know if it was kept.

terms.meaning: A group of people who live near each other, share places and things, and depend on each other.
terms.example: The 40 families of one apartment block in Chennai, with their watchman, their sweeper and the shop at the gate, are a community.
terms.art: Families on the balconies of one building waving to each other, with a small shop at the gate.

terms.meaning: The streets and buildings near your home, and the people in them.
terms.example: Lakshmi's neighbourhood in Madurai has her school, a temple, a ration shop, a tailor and a bus stop, all within a short walk.
terms.art: A simple map of a few streets with a home, a school, a shop and a bus stop marked.

terms.meaning: The work a person does to earn a living, which needs skill and learning.
terms.example: Divya's Athai is a nurse. Her neighbour is a tailor. Nursing and tailoring are professions.
terms.art: A nurse with a blood pressure cuff and a tailor at a sewing machine, side by side.

terms.meaning: The way a person earns the money or food they need to live.
terms.example: The flower seller at the temple gate earns her livelihood by stringing and selling jasmine.
terms.art: A woman stringing jasmine flowers at a small stall outside a temple.

terms.meaning: To need someone or something to live or to do your work.
terms.example: The idli shop depends on the farmer for rice, on the gas delivery man for a cylinder and on the municipality for water.
terms.art: A plate of idlis with arrows to a rice field, a gas cylinder and a tap.

terms.meaning: A service set up for everyone in a place, such as a government school, a health centre, the post office or the water supply.
terms.example: Arjun's water comes from the city's water board, and his baby sister got her vaccines free at the government health centre. Both are public services.
terms.art: A government health centre with a red cross sign and a queue of mothers holding babies.

terms.meaning: Money that people and shops pay to the government, which it uses to run public services.
terms.example: When Amma buys a packet of biscuits, part of the price is a tax called GST. Some of that money helps pay for roads, schools and hospitals.
terms.art: A shop bill with a line marked 'GST', and arrows to a road, a school and a hospital.

terms.meaning: The local government of a town or city. It looks after water, drains, roads, street lights, garbage and the record of births. A big city has a municipal corporation.
terms.example: The Greater Chennai Corporation sends the garbage collectors who come to Revathi's street every morning.
terms.art: A municipal garbage van with workers in uniform collecting bags from a street.

terms.meaning: The elected local government of a village. It looks after village roads, water, cleanliness and other shared work.
terms.example: In Farhan's grandfather's village near Mysuru, the gram panchayat repaired the hand pump and cleaned the village pond.
terms.art: A village meeting under a tree, with women and men sitting together and a hand pump nearby.

terms.meaning: Something useful that many people use together and nobody owns alone, such as a pond, a park, a lift or the fish in the sea. Scientists also call this a commons.
terms.example: The overhead tank in a building is a shared resource. Water one flat uses is water another flat cannot use.
terms.art: A water tank on a roof with pipes going down to twelve flats.

terms.meaning: An agreement about what people may and may not do, which everyone knows.
terms.example: In Kavya's building, the rule says nobody washes cars with tank water in summer.
terms.art: A notice board in a building lobby with a few short rules written on it.

terms.meaning: To work together towards something that helps everyone.
terms.example: The families in Meenakshi's lane cooperate to keep the drain clear before the rains.
terms.art: Neighbours together clearing leaves from a drain on a street before the rains.

terms.meaning: The idea that every honest job deserves respect, whether it is done with the hands or with the head.
terms.example: The sweeper who cleans the street and the doctor at the clinic both do work the neighbourhood cannot live without.
terms.art: A sweeper and a doctor shaking hands on a clean street.

terms.meaning: A sudden danger to someone's life, health or home, which needs help at once.
terms.example: A fire in a kitchen, a person who has fallen and will not wake, or a serious accident on the road is an emergency. In India, the number to call is 112.
terms.art: A phone screen showing the number 112.

explanations.context: This card is about what turns people who live near each other into a community.
explanations.definition: A community is a group of people who live near each other, share places and things, and depend on each other.
explanations.description: A family is a small group of people who care for each other. A community is bigger. It is the families of a building, a street or a village, and the people who work there. They share roads, water, a market and a school. They also share problems, such as a blocked drain or a dry tank. Nobody in a community can meet all their needs alone.
examples: An apartment block in Chennai, with its families, its watchman and its residents' association.
A fishing village near Kochi, where families share the boats, the beach and the market.
The people who live and work around one market in Hyderabad.
explanations.art: A street seen from above, with houses, a shop, a school and a tank, joined by dotted lines between the people.

explanations.concept: Why we depend on each other's work
explanations.context: This card is about why a neighbourhood needs so many different jobs.
explanations.definition: Interdependence means that people need each other's work. When each person does one kind of work and gets good at it, everyone can have more than they could make alone.
explanations.description: Think of one plate of idli. A farmer grew the rice and the urad dal. A truck driver brought them to the city. A shopkeeper sold them. A factory worker filled the gas cylinder, and a delivery man carried it up the stairs. The water came through the city's pipes. Nobody could do all of this alone. Each person learns one kind of work well. In return, they get what other people make.
examples: A tailor stitches clothes for the farmer, and the farmer grows rice for the tailor.
A doctor cannot work if nobody cleans the hospital.
A postwoman carries letters for the whole street, so each family does not have to travel.
explanations.art: A plate of idlis in the middle, with lines out to a farmer, a truck driver, a shopkeeper, a gas delivery man and a tap.

explanations.concept: Every job needs skill, and every worker deserves respect
explanations.context: This card is about why no honest work is small, and why a person may choose their work.
explanations.definition: Dignity of labour is the idea that every honest job deserves respect. In India, the Constitution gives every citizen the right to choose their work.
explanations.description: Some jobs look simple from outside. Try stringing jasmine as fast as the flower seller, or ironing a shirt as smoothly as the presswala, and you find how much skill they need. For a long time in India, many people were expected to do only the work their family did. Some were called 'untouchable' and kept out of schools and wells. Dr B.R. Ambedkar faced this as a child. He led the writing of India's Constitution, which came into force in 1950. It ended untouchability and gives every person the right to choose their work.
examples: A sweeper who clears a drain before the rains stops the street from flooding.
A nurse learns for years before she can work in a hospital.
Ambedkar's father worked in the army, and Ambedkar became a lawyer, an economist and a writer of the Constitution.
explanations.art: A row of workers' hands: a hand stringing jasmine, a hand holding an iron, a hand writing, a hand holding a broom.

explanations.context: This card is about the services set up for everyone, and who pays for them.
explanations.definition: A public service is a service set up for everyone in a place, usually by the government, such as a school, a health centre, the post office, the water supply, garbage collection, the police and the fire service.
explanations.description: Some things are too big for one family to arrange. A family cannot build its own water pipe from a lake, or train its own fire service. So the government runs these for everyone. It pays for them with taxes. Taxes are money that people and shops pay to the government. Most things bought in a shop include a tax called GST, so even a child buying a pencil helps pay. A government health centre gives children their vaccines free. A government school teaches children free up to Class 8. The post office carries letters to every corner of India.
examples: The Greater Chennai Corporation collects garbage from the streets.
The fire service comes when you call 101 or 112.
The government health centre gives babies their vaccines free.
explanations.art: Small pictures of a school, a health centre, a post office, a fire engine, a garbage van and a water pipe, arranged in a circle around a coin marked 'tax'.

explanations.concept: Who to call in an emergency
explanations.context: This card is about the numbers that bring help fast.
explanations.definition: 112 is India's single emergency number. One call to 112 can bring the police, the fire service or an ambulance.
explanations.description: An emergency is a sudden danger to someone's life, health or home. In an emergency, call 112. Say your name, what has happened and your full address, slowly. Many states also have 108 for an ambulance and 101 for the fire service. 1098 is the helpline for any child who needs help. These numbers are only for real emergencies, because someone else may need the ambulance at the same moment.
examples: Paati has fallen and is not waking up: call 112 or 108.
Smoke is coming from a flat downstairs: call 112 or 101.
A child is being hurt by a grown-up: call 1098.
explanations.art: A card stuck by a door with 112, 108, 101 and 1098 written on it, and a space for the home address.

explanations.context: This card is about things that many people use and nobody owns alone.
explanations.definition: A shared resource, also called a commons, is something useful that many people use together, where what one person takes is not there for the next.
explanations.description: A water tank, a village pond, a park, a lift, a parking space, the fish in the sea and the clean air of a city are shared resources. They are different from a pencil, which is yours alone. They are also different from a song on the radio. Your listening does not leave less song for anyone else. With a shared resource, every bucket one flat fills is water the other flats cannot use. That is why a shared thing can run out.
examples: The overhead tank of an apartment block.
The eri, the old rain-fed tanks of Tamil Nadu villages, which farmers shared for watering fields.
The fish off the coast of Kerala, caught by many boats.
explanations.art: A village tank in Tamil Nadu with a stone sluice, fields around it and several farmers standing at its edge.

explanations.concept: Why some shared things run out and others last
explanations.context: This card is about a real argument among scientists. Can people who share a thing keep it from running out?
explanations.description: Some shared things are spoiled, like rivers full of waste. Others have lasted for hundreds of years, like meadows and water channels shared by whole villages. Scientists argued about why. Here are the main views.
examples: In the Shared Pond Test, the silent game often ends with an empty pond.
The farmers of Törbel, a village in Switzerland, have shared their mountain meadows under rules written down since at least 1517.
Many fish in the sea are still caught faster than they breed.

perspectives.who: Garrett Hardin, an American ecologist, in 1968
perspectives.explanation: Each person gets the whole gain from taking a bit more, and shares the loss with everyone. So each person keeps taking more, and the shared thing is ruined. Only a government or an owner can stop this.

perspectives.who: Elinor Ostrom, an American political scientist, from the 1970s to 2012
perspectives.explanation: Many communities make their own rules and look after shared things for centuries. They do best when they make the rules together, someone watches that the rules are kept, and breaking a rule has a small cost.
Both can happen. Small groups who know each other, and can talk, often look after a shared thing well. Very big shared things, like the sea or the air, with millions of strangers, are much harder.

explanations.art: Two ponds side by side: one dried and cracked with people arguing, one full with people sitting together around a written rule.

explanations.concept: What helps a shared thing last
explanations.context: This card is about the rules Elinor Ostrom found in communities whose shared things lasted.
explanations.definition: Elinor Ostrom found that shared things last best when everyone knows who shares them, the users make the rules together, someone checks the rules are kept, breaking a rule has a small cost that grows, and there is a fair way to settle quarrels.
explanations.description: Ostrom studied village meadows, forests, fishing grounds and water channels in many countries, including farmers sharing water channels in Nepal. Where the shared thing lasted, the same kinds of rules kept appearing. In old Tamil Nadu villages, a water keeper called the neerkatti opened the tank's sluice for each field in turn. Your building's notice board, the turn for the lift and the time for the water motor are rules of the same kind.
examples: A building where the caretaker writes down who used the tank motor, and when.
A fishing village that agrees not to fish in the months when the fish breed.
Children at a park who agree on turns for the one swing.
explanations.art: An old water keeper opening a wooden sluice gate on a village tank while farmers wait their turn.

agreed.text: No person or family can meet all their needs alone. People depend on each other's work.
agreed.evidence: Every city and village has many kinds of work, and studies of trade and work everywhere show it.

agreed.text: Shared resources can be used up when each person takes as much as they like.
agreed.evidence: Fish catches have fallen in many seas, and many city lakes have shrunk. In the Shared Pond Test, the silent game often empties the pond.

agreed.text: Many communities have looked after shared resources for hundreds of years with rules they made themselves.
agreed.evidence: Elinor Ostrom's studies of meadows in Switzerland, water channels in Spain and Nepal, and forests and fishing grounds in many countries.

agreed.text: People who can talk to each other share a resource better than people who cannot.
agreed.evidence: In laboratory tests by Ostrom, Roy Gardner and James Walker in the early 1990s, groups allowed to talk took far less from a shared pool than groups kept silent.

agreed.text: Vaccines given free through public health centres have saved millions of children's lives in India.
agreed.evidence: India's national vaccination programme for children. Gagandeep Kang helped develop Rotavac, a vaccine made in India against rotavirus, which causes severe diarrhoea in babies. It joined the programme in 2016.

challenging.claim: Some jobs are high and some are low.
challenging.who: A common view, and the old caste system
challenging.context: This card is about whether some honest work is worth less than other work.
challenging.for: Some jobs are paid much more, and some need many years at college.
challenging.against: Every job needs skill, and the neighbourhood falls apart without any of them. A street floods if nobody clears the drain. India's Constitution ended untouchability and gives everyone the right to choose their work.

challenging.claim: A shared thing will always be ruined, unless a government or an owner controls it.
challenging.who: Garrett Hardin, The Tragedy of the Commons, 1968
challenging.context: This card is about whether people who share a thing can look after it themselves.
challenging.for: Many shared things have been ruined, such as polluted rivers and empty fishing grounds.
challenging.against: Elinor Ostrom found many villages that have looked after meadows, forests and water for centuries with their own rules. Hardin himself later said he should have called it the tragedy of the unmanaged commons.

challenging.claim: Public services should be run by private companies, not the government.
challenging.context: This card is about who should run services such as water and buses.
challenging.for: Companies that must win customers may work faster and waste less.
challenging.against: A company may not serve places where it cannot make money, such as a far village. Services like clean water and vaccines must reach everyone, rich or poor.

challenging.claim: Machines will soon do the work of most helpers.
challenging.context: This card is about whether machines will replace people's work.
challenging.for: Washing machines, ATMs and online shopping already do work that people once did.
challenging.against: New kinds of work also appear, such as delivery riders and phone repairers. Caring work, like nursing, is hard for a machine. Nobody knows how this will go.

big_questions.q: When the pond ran out in the silent game, whose fault was it?
big_questions.hint: Each player took only what they thought was fair for themself. Think about what each one could see.

big_questions.q: Is the air of a city a shared resource? Who makes the rules for it?
big_questions.hint: Think about who breathes it, who fills it with smoke, and whether they can talk to each other.

big_questions.q: Why do we say thank you to a shopkeeper we pay, but not to a sweeper who is paid by the city?
big_questions.hint: Think about whose work you see being done for you.

big_questions.q: If everyone in your building talked for five minutes, would the tank stop running dry?
big_questions.hint: Remember the talking game. What else did it need besides the talk?

big_questions.q: Should a child have a say in the rules of the building?
big_questions.hint: Children use the lift, the park and the water too.

big_questions.q: Is a road a shared thing, like a pond? What runs out on a road?
big_questions.hint: Think about space, at the busiest time of day.

story.title: The Tank on the Roof
story.note: The story is made up. What it shows is true: shared water often runs short in Indian cities in summer, Tamil Nadu villages once had water keepers called neerkattis, and groups who agree rules together share a resource better.
text: Revathi was nine, and she lived on the third floor of Thendral Apartments in Chennai. There were twelve flats in the building, and one big water tank on the roof.

Every morning in summer, a blue water lorry came to the gate. It filled the sump, the tank under the ground. Then Selvi akka, the caretaker, switched on the motor. The motor pumped the water up to the tank on the roof, and pipes took it down to every flat.

That May, something went wrong. By two o'clock each afternoon, the taps on the third floor gave only air. Revathi's Amma came home from the hospital, where she was a nurse, and found no water to wash her hands.

"Someone on the ground floor washes their car with a hose," said Mr Raghavan from flat 4. "Someone fills six drums every morning," said the family in flat 9. Everybody was sure someone else was taking too much. Nobody thought it was them.

That night, Revathi's Paati sat on the mat and listened to all of this. Then she said, "In my village near Kanchipuram, we had an eri. A big rain tank, for all the fields. It never ran dry before the harvest."
"Why not?" asked Revathi. "Didn't everyone take what they wanted?"

"No," said Paati. "We had a neerkatti. He was the water keeper. He opened the sluice for one field, then the next, in turn. Everyone knew the order. If a farmer cut the bank to steal water, the whole village knew by evening. The farmers paid the neerkatti with a share of their harvest."
Revathi thought about it. "But the neerkatti was only one man. Why did everyone listen to him?"
"Because we chose the rules together, at the village meeting," said Paati. "A rule you make yourself is easier to keep."

The next day, Revathi tried a test her Amma had read about. She poured twenty chana into a steel bowl. "These are fish in a pond," she said. "Each round, everyone writes how many fish they take, up to five. Then the fish left in the pond have babies, and the pond doubles. But a pond can only hold twenty."

Amma, Paati and her little brother Karthik played. In the first game, nobody was allowed to speak. Karthik wrote 5. Amma wrote 5. Paati wrote 4, and Revathi wrote 5. That left only one fish. One fish became two. In the second round, there were not enough fish for everyone, and the pond was empty.
"I only took my share," said Karthik, surprised.
"So did I," said Amma. "That is the trouble."

In the second game, they were allowed to talk first. Paati did the sums out loud. "If we leave at least ten fish, they double back to twenty. So together we can take ten each round, no more." They agreed: two each, and Paati would count the bowl after every round. They played six rounds. The pond stayed full to the end. When they added up, each of them had caught twelve fish, far more than in the silent game.
Revathi wrote both results in her notebook, in two neat tables.
On Sunday, the residents' association met in the parking area. Mr Raghavan was the secretary. People started to argue again. Revathi stood up, holding her notebook, and her voice shook a little.

"Uncle, can I show you something?" she asked. She explained the two games to Mr Raghavan, and showed him the tables. "When nobody talked, the pond was empty in two rounds. When we made a rule together, it lasted. The tank is our pond."
Mr Raghavan read the tables twice. "What rule would you make?" he asked.

Revathi and Paati had thought about this. "No car washing with tank water until the rains," said Revathi. "Each flat fills its drums only once a day. And Selvi akka writes in a notebook when the motor runs, and how full the tank is at two o'clock. Everyone can read the notebook."
"And if someone breaks the rule?" asked flat 9.
"The first time, Selvi akka just tells them," said Paati. "The second time, the meeting talks about it."
They voted. Eleven flats said yes. One flat said they would try it for a week.
That week, Selvi akka's notebook showed something new. At two o'clock, the tank was still half full. On Friday, Amma came home and washed her hands under a running tap. She smiled at Revathi.
"The lorry brought the same water as last week," said Revathi. "We just shared it differently."
Selvi akka laughed. "So now I am the neerkatti of Thendral Apartments," she said.
story.epiphany: The same water can run out by afternoon or last all day. What changed was not the water but the rules the families made together, and someone keeping watch.
ask: Why did the tank run dry, even though the lorry came every morning?
Karthik said, "I only took my share." Why did the pond still run out?
What did the neerkatti do in Paati's village, and why did the farmers listen to him?
Which part of the new rule do you think mattered most: no car washing, filling drums once, or Selvi akka's notebook? Why?

printables.title: Score sheet
items: A helper I did not know about

rules: Shuffle the problem cards and put them in a pile, problem side up.
On your turn, take the top card and read the problem aloud.
Say who helps with it, and what they do.
Turn the card over and read the back. If you were right, keep the card. If not, put it at the bottom of the pile.
When the pile is empty, the player with the most cards wins. Playing alone with one grown-up, try to beat your own score next time.

experiments.title: The Shared Pond Test: does agreeing a rule keep a pond from running out?
experiments.context: In this experiment your family shares a pond of chana fish. You play once without talking and once after agreeing a rule, and see which pond lasts.
experiments.question: When people share a pond, does it last longer if they talk and agree a rule first?
experiments.predict: Guess first. In which game will the pond last longer: the silent game, or the game where you talk first? Will anyone end up with more fish in one game? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Play both games with the same people, the same 20 fish, the same limit on how many each player may take, and the same 6 rounds. In both games, every player tries to end up with as many fish as they can. Only one thing changes: in the second game, players may talk and agree a rule before they choose. Everyone still writes their choice in secret, so nobody is forced.
results_table: Fish in the pond at the start
Fish after the pond doubles (no more than 20)

materials.item: dried chana, rajma or tamarind seeds, as fish
a steel bowl, as the pond
small slips of paper and a pencil for each player
a notebook for the results table
3 or 4 players: the child and family members

experiments.safety: Nothing in this experiment is unsafe. Younger brothers and sisters under 3 should not have dried chana, which they could choke on.

schedule.what: Guess first. Play the silent game for up to 6 rounds, then the talking game for 6 rounds. Fill in the table and compare the two games.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table for both games. Add up how many fish each player caught in each game. Draw a line for each game, showing the fish in the pond after each round.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Shared Pond Test. You learn the rules and make your guess.
flow.do: 1. Put 20 chana in the steel bowl. 2. Give each player 12 paper slips and a pencil. 3. Read the rules aloud. 4. Write your child's guess and reason in the notebook.
flow.say: These 20 chana are fish in a pond we all share. Each round, you secretly write how many fish you take, from 0 to 5. Then the fish left in the pond have babies, so the pond doubles. But the pond can never hold more than 20. If it ever reaches 0, no fish are left to have babies. Your aim is to catch as many fish as you can. Which game will last longer, silent or talking? Why?
flow.kid: The chana are fish. Each round, write how many you take, 0 to 5. The fish left will double. The pond holds 20 at most. Guess: will the silent game or the talking game last longer? Why?

ask.q: Which game do you think will last longer, and why?
good: The talking game, because we can agree not to take too much.
The same, because everyone wants fish in both games.

flow.parent: With 2 players, let each take up to 8 fish a round. With 5 or more, up to 3. This keeps the test fair. Write the guess down before you start, because a wrong guess is a useful result too.

flow.context: This is the silent game of the Shared Pond Test. Nobody may speak until it ends.
flow.do: 1. Each round, every player writes a number from 0 to 5 on a slip, folds it and puts it down. 2. Open the slips together. 3. Each player takes that many fish. If there are not enough, take turns picking one fish at a time, youngest first, until the pond is empty. 4. Count the fish left, double them, and add fish from the spare pile, up to 20. 5. Your child writes the round in the table. 6. Play 6 rounds, or stop when the pond is empty.
flow.say: No talking in this game. Write your number and fold the slip. Ready? Open them. How many fish are left? Double them. That is the pond for the next round.
flow.kid: No talking. Write your number. Fold it. Open together. Take your fish. Count what is left, then double it.
flow.parent: Grown-ups should really try to catch the most fish for themselves, as they would in any game. Do not hold back to help the child win, or the test will not be fair. With 4 players taking 5 each, the pond usually empties in one or two rounds. If your pond lasts, that is a real result: ask why later.

check.q: There are 6 fish left in the pond after a round. The fish left double. How many fish are in the pond for the next round?
check.why: Doubling means two times as many. 6 and 6 make 12. The pond only stops at 20 when doubling would give more than 20. If you chose 20, you filled the pond to the top, but 12 is less than 20.

flow.context: This is the break between the two games of the Shared Pond Test.
flow.do: 1. Each player counts the fish they caught in the silent game. 2. Write each total in the notebook. 3. Put all the fish back, so the pond has 20 again.
flow.say: How many fish did each of us catch? How many rounds did the pond last?
flow.kid: Count your fish. Write your total. Put the fish back. The pond has 20 again.

flow.context: This is the talking time before the second game of the Shared Pond Test.
flow.do: 1. Give the players 3 minutes to talk. 2. Let them agree a rule, if they want one. 3. Write the rule in the notebook.
flow.say: Now we may talk for 3 minutes before we play. Is there a rule that would help? How many fish can we all take each round and still have 20 next time?
flow.kid: Now you may talk. Can you agree a rule? How many fish can you all take and still keep the pond full?

ask.q: How many fish must stay in the pond so it doubles back to 20?

flow.parent: Let your child lead the talk if they can. Do not give them the answer. If nobody sees it, ask: 'If 10 fish stay in the pond, how many will there be after doubling?' A rule usually sounds like: 'We take 10 fish in all each round, so 2 or 3 each.' Some families also choose a person to count the pond after each round.

flow.context: This is the talking game of the Shared Pond Test. You play with the rule you agreed.
flow.do: 1. Play 6 rounds exactly as before: secret slips, open together, take fish, double what is left. 2. Players may now talk between rounds too. 3. Your child writes each round in the table.
flow.say: Same rules as before, but now we have our rule. Still write your number in secret. Did everyone keep the rule this round?
flow.kid: Same game. Write your number in secret. Did everyone keep the rule?
flow.parent: Grown-ups still try to catch as many fish as they can, but they may now keep or break the rule as they really would. If someone breaks it, let the players talk about it. That is part of the test.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Shared Pond Test. You compare the two games and explain what you found.
flow.do: 1. Each player counts their fish from the talking game. 2. Compare both tables. 3. Ask your child for a claim, the evidence and a reason. 4. Compare with the guess from the start.
flow.say: In which game did the pond last longer? In which game did each of us catch more fish? What changed between the two games? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Which pond lasted longer? When did you catch more fish? What was different? Was your guess right?

ask.q: Why did the pond run out, or last, in each game?
good: In the silent game everyone took a lot, so too few fish were left to double.
In the talking game we took 10 in all each round, so 10 stayed and doubled back to 20.
We caught more in the talking game, because the pond kept making fish.

flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: talking and agreeing a rule kept the pond full. What I saw: the silent pond was empty after 2 rounds, and the talking pond lasted all 6. Why: we left at least 10 fish each time, so the pond doubled back to 20.
flow.think: Our building's water tank is a shared pond too. What would a rule for it look like?

experiments.title: The Postcard Test: how many days does a letter take, and how many people carry it?
experiments.context: In this experiment you post a postcard to a relative in another town and count how many days it takes to arrive.
experiments.question: How many days does a postcard take to reach a relative in another town, and what does the post office do on the way?
experiments.predict: Guess first. How many days will your postcard take to arrive? Will a card to a far town take longer than a card to a near one? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Write the full address with the PIN code clearly, so the card is not slowed by a mistake. Post it on a working day, and write the date you post it. Ask the relative to phone you the day it arrives. If you can, send two cards on the same day, one to a near town and one to a far town, so the distance is the only big difference.

materials.item: a postcard from the post office, or an envelope with a stamp
a pen
the full address and PIN code of a relative in another town
a calendar

experiments.safety: A grown-up goes with the child to the post box or the post office.

schedule.what: Guess first. Write the postcard with the full address and PIN code. Post it with a grown-up and write the date.
Ask: has the relative phoned yet? Write 'not yet' or the date.
Count the days the card took. Compare with your guess, and talk about what the post office did.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the path of the card: post box, post office, sorting office, train or van, the town's post office, and the postwoman or postman at the door.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Postcard Test. You write the card and guess how long it will take.
flow.do: 1. Your child writes a short message to a relative in another town. 2. Write the full address and the 6-digit PIN code. 3. Write the guess and reason in the table.
flow.say: Write to Ammamma: 'I am testing the post office. Please phone us the day this card reaches you.' How many days do you think it will take? Why?
flow.kid: Write to your relative. Ask them to phone when it comes. Write the PIN code. Guess how many days. Why?
flow.parent: PIN stands for Postal Index Number. The first digit tells the region of India. Chennai PIN codes begin with 6, and Delhi PIN codes begin with 1.

flow.context: This is the posting step of the Postcard Test.
flow.do: 1. Walk with your child to a red post box or a post office. 2. Read the collection times on the box. 3. Post the card. 4. Write today's date in the table.
flow.say: Look at the times on the box. When will the postman collect our card? Let's write today's date.
flow.kid: Read the times on the post box. Post your card. Write today's date.
flow.parent: If you are inside a post office, point out the counter for stamps, the savings counter and the bags of letters.

flow.context: This is the waiting part of the Postcard Test.
flow.do: Each check day, ask your child whether the relative has phoned. Write 'not yet' or the date it arrived.
flow.say: Has Ammamma phoned? Let's write it on the calendar.
flow.kid: Has the card arrived? Write it on the calendar.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Postcard Test. You count the days and think about who carried your card.
flow.do: 1. Count the days from posting to arriving. 2. Compare with the guess. 3. Draw the card's path and count the people who handled it.
flow.say: How many days did it take? Was your guess close? How many people do you think touched our card on the way?
flow.kid: Count the days. Was your guess close? Draw the card's path. Who carried it?

ask.q: What could make a card slower?
good: A far village where the post comes only some days.

flow.parent: A card often passes through a post box collector, a sorting office, a mail van or a train, another sorting office and a delivery person. That is at least five people, all paid from the stamp and from taxes.

check.q: Lakshmi posts a card in Madurai on Monday. It reaches her Athai in Kochi on Thursday. How many days did it take?
check.why: Count on from Monday: Tuesday is 1, Wednesday is 2, Thursday is 3. If you chose 4, you counted Monday as well.

activities.title: Who Keeps Our Building Going? A list of the helpers we hardly see
activities.context: In this activity you list every person whose work keeps your home and building going, and sort them by what they do.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil
coloured pencils

activities.safety: Nothing in this activity is unsafe.

schedule.what: Who Keeps Our Building Going? A list of the helpers we hardly see

activities.record: A list of helpers sorted into five groups: food, water, cleaning, health and safety, and messages and things.

flow.context: This is a short activity to start the unit. You list the helpers your home depends on.
flow.do: 1. Ask your child to think about yesterday, from waking up to bedtime. 2. List every person whose work they used, seen or unseen. 3. Write each one down.
flow.say: Who brought the milk packet? Who collected the garbage? Who sent the water to our taps? Who drove the bus? Let's write every one.
flow.kid: Think about yesterday. Who brought the milk? Who took the garbage? Who sent the water? Write each one.
flow.parent: Help your child think of people they never see: the person who fills the gas cylinder, the electricity lineman, the farmer, the water board worker. Most families reach 15 to 25 people.

flow.context: This is the sorting step of the helpers list.
flow.do: Draw five boxes: food, water, cleaning, health and safety, messages and things. Sort each helper into a box.
flow.say: Which box does the sweeper go in? And the postwoman? Which box has the most people?
flow.kid: Draw five boxes. Put each helper in a box. Which box is fullest?

check.q: Selvi akka is the caretaker of a building. She switches on the motor that pumps water to the tank on the roof. Which box does she go in?
check.why: She brings water to every flat, so she goes in the water box. Some helpers fit more than one box. A strong sorter says why.

flow.context: This is the last step of the helpers list. You think about what would happen without one helper.
flow.do: Your child picks one helper and says what would happen if that person did not come for a week.
flow.say: Pick one helper. What would our home be like if they did not come for a week?
flow.kid: Pick one helper. What if they did not come for a week?

ask.q: What would happen without the garbage collector for a week?
good: The bins would overflow and smell.
Flies and rats would come, and people could get sick.

flow.think: Which of these helpers have you never thanked?

activities.title: Meet a Helper: a short interview with a worker near home
activities.context: In this activity you meet one worker near your home, ask them three questions and draw them at their work.

materials.item: a notebook and crayons
a little money to buy something small or to get clothes ironed

activities.safety: A grown-up goes with the child and stays with them the whole time.

schedule.what: Meet a Helper: a short interview with a worker near home

activities.record: A drawing of the worker with their tool, their name, their work and one thing they said.

flow.context: This is the first step of Meet a Helper. You choose a worker and practise your questions.
flow.do: 1. Choose one worker near home: the presswala, the tailor, the cobbler, the flower seller or the vegetable seller. 2. Practise three polite questions.
flow.say: Let's practise. 'What is your work called? Who taught you? What is the hardest part of your work?'
flow.kid: Choose a helper. Practise three questions. What is your work? Who taught you? What is hardest?

flow.context: This is the visit for Meet a Helper.
flow.do: 1. Walk to the worker with your child. 2. Buy something small or get one shirt ironed, so you are customers. 3. Your child greets them, asks the questions and thanks them by name.
flow.say: Vanakkam. My daughter is learning about the people who work in our neighbourhood. Could she ask you three quick questions?
flow.kid: Greet them. Ask your three questions. Listen. Say thank you, with their name.
flow.parent: Choose a quiet time, when the worker is not busy. If they would rather not answer, thank them and leave it. That is their right.

flow.context: This is the last step of Meet a Helper. You draw what you learned.
flow.do: At home, your child draws the worker with their tool and writes their name, their work and one thing they said.
flow.say: What surprised you? How long did they take to learn their work?
flow.kid: Draw the helper and their tool. Write their name and one thing they said.

ask.q: What did you learn about their work?
good: The presswala learned from his mother when he was young.
The flower seller starts at 5 in the morning.

flow.think: Could you do their work tomorrow? What would you need to learn?

activities.title: Our Emergency Card: who to call, and what to say
activities.context: In this activity you make a card of emergency numbers and practise a pretend call.

materials.item: a piece of card from an old box
a sketch pen
tape

activities.safety: The child must only practise with the phone switched off or locked. Real calls are only for real emergencies.

schedule.what: Our Emergency Card: who to call, and what to say

activities.record: An emergency card stuck near the door, and one practised call.

flow.context: This is the first step of Our Emergency Card. You write the numbers that bring help.
flow.do: 1. Write on the card: 112 for police, fire and ambulance. 108 for an ambulance. 101 for fire. 1098 for any child who needs help. 2. Add a parent's number, a neighbour's number and the full home address.
flow.say: 112 is the one number to remember. It brings the police, the fire service or an ambulance. Let's write our address too, because the helper needs to find us.
flow.kid: Write 112, 108, 101 and 1098. Write a parent's number. Write your full address.

flow.context: This is the practice call for Our Emergency Card.
flow.do: With the phone off, your child practises a call. They say their name, what happened and the address, slowly.
flow.say: Let's pretend Paati has fallen and is not waking up. Say: 'My name is Revathi. My Paati has fallen and is not waking up. Our address is flat 9, Thendral Apartments...'
flow.kid: Pretend to call. Say your name. Say what happened. Say your address slowly.

check.q: Which of these is a real emergency?
options: Smoke is coming from the flat below
check.why: Smoke can mean a fire, which puts lives in danger. That is an emergency, so call 112. A lost pencil or a broken television is a problem, but nobody's life is in danger.

flow.context: This is the last step of Our Emergency Card.
flow.do: Stick the card near the door.
flow.say: Why must we only call these numbers in a real emergency?
flow.kid: Stick the card by the door. Why only call in a real emergency?

ask.q: Why only in a real emergency?
good: Someone else might need the ambulance at the same time.

activities.title: The Water Trail: where does our tap water come from?
activities.context: In this activity you follow the water in your home backwards, from the tap to where it began.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a phone map, if you have one

activities.safety: A grown-up goes with the child to see the sump, the motor or the tank. The child never climbs onto a tank or opens a sump lid.

schedule.what: The Water Trail: where does our tap water come from?

activities.record: A drawing of the water's path from the tap back to a lake, a river or the ground, with each helper on the way.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Water Trail. You find where water enters your building.
flow.do: 1. With your child, find the pipe that brings water into your building. 2. Look for the sump, the motor and the tank on the roof. 3. Ask the watchman or caretaker where the water comes from: a city pipe, a borewell or a lorry.
flow.say: Water comes to our tap through a pipe. Let's follow it. Where does it come into the building?
flow.kid: Follow the pipe from your tap. Find the motor and the tank. Ask where the water comes from.
flow.parent: In many cities, water comes partly from the city water board and partly from a borewell or water lorries.

flow.context: This is the second step of the Water Trail. You find the lake or river your city uses.
flow.do: Find out which lakes or rivers your city's water comes from. Look on your city water board's website or ask a neighbour.
flow.say: Chennai's water comes from lakes such as Puzhal and Chembarambakkam, and from plants that take the salt out of sea water. Bengaluru's comes mostly from the Kaveri river. Where does ours come from?
flow.kid: Which lake or river sends water to your city? Find out with a grown-up.
flow.parent: If you cannot find it, write 'from a lake or river, brought by the city's pipes'. The idea is what matters.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Water Trail. You draw the whole path.
flow.do: Your child draws the path from the lake or river to the tap, and draws one helper at each stage.
flow.say: Who works at each stage? Who cleans the water? Who mends a burst pipe?
flow.kid: Draw the water's path. Draw a helper at each stage.
flow.think: The lake is shared by a whole city. What happens if one part of the city uses too much?

activities.title: The Rule Hunt: find the rules for our shared things
activities.context: In this activity you find the rules for the shared things in your building, and work out why each one is there.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up goes with the child around the building.

schedule.what: The Rule Hunt: find the rules for our shared things

activities.record: A table of shared things, their rules, who made them and why.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Rule Hunt. You look for written rules in your building.
flow.do: Walk around the building with your child. Look at the notice board, the lift, the gate, the parking area and the terrace. Write each rule you find.
flow.say: Look at the lift. Is there a rule? How many people can go in at once? What about the terrace door?
flow.kid: Look for rules on the notice board, the lift and the gate. Write each one.
flow.parent: If you live in a house, look at the rules of a park, a temple, a bus or the street instead.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Rule Hunt. You work out why each rule is there.
flow.do: Make a table: the shared thing, the rule, who made it and why. Talk about one rule that is often broken.
flow.say: Why do you think this rule is here? What would happen without it? Who checks that it is kept?
flow.kid: Why is each rule there? What if nobody kept it? Who checks?

check.q: The lift in Nandini's building says 'No more than 6 people'. Why is the rule there?
options: So the lift is not too heavy to carry safely
So the lift is more fun
check.why: A lift is made to carry only a certain weight safely. The rule keeps the shared lift safe for everyone. Many rules for shared things keep them safe or stop them running out.

projects.title: The Corridor Plant: share one plant for a week with a turn list
projects.context: In this week-long project, several people share the care of one potted plant, with a rule and a turn list, and see whether the plant does well.

materials.item: one potted plant in a corridor, on a landing or by the door
a mug for watering
a sheet of paper for the turn list, and a pencil on a string

projects.safety: Ask the neighbours' parents before a child knocks on a neighbour's door. A grown-up helps move the pot if it is heavy.

schedule.what: Choose a shared plant. Meet the people who will share it: neighbours' children or your family. Agree a rule and make a turn list.
Check the turn list and the soil.
Check the turn list and the soil.
Check the turn list and the soil.
Check the turn list and the soil.
Check the turn list and the soil.
Meet again. Look at the plant and the turn list. Was the rule kept? Change it if needed.

projects.record: The turn list with ticks, a note each day on whether the soil was dry, damp or soggy, and a drawing of the plant on day 1 and day 7.

flow.context: This is the first day of the Corridor Plant project. You agree how to share the care of one plant.
flow.do: 1. Choose one plant that several people pass every day. 2. Meet with the others who will share it. 3. Agree a rule together, for example 'one mug of water when the soil is dry, one person each day'. 4. Make a turn list with the days and names, and a box to tick.
flow.say: This plant belongs to all of us. If nobody waters it, it dries out. If everyone waters it, it drowns. What rule should we make?
flow.kid: Many people share this plant. Too little water dries it. Too much drowns it. Make a rule together.
flow.parent: If there are no neighbours' children, share the plant within the family: each person has a day. The point is to see whether a shared plant does well with a rule and a list.

flow.wait: Do this each day from day 2 to day 6
flow.context: This is the daily check in the Corridor Plant project.
flow.do: Each day, your child checks the turn list and touches the soil. They write 'dry', 'damp' or 'soggy'.
flow.say: Whose turn was it yesterday? Did they tick? How does the soil feel?
flow.kid: Check the list. Touch the soil. Write dry, damp or soggy.

flow.context: This is the last day of the Corridor Plant project.
flow.do: Meet again. Look at the plant and the list. Ask each person what was easy and hard. Change the rule if it did not work.
flow.say: Is the plant doing well? Did everyone keep the rule? What would make it work better?
flow.kid: Look at the plant and the list. Was the rule kept? Should we change it?
flow.think: Who checked that the rule was kept? Did that help?

challenges.title: Fair Water for Twelve Flats
challenges.context: This is a planning challenge. You make a fair rule so that every flat in a building gets water in summer.
challenges.problem: A building has 12 flats and one tank on the roof. In summer, the tank fills only once a day, in the morning. By afternoon, the top floor has no water. Make a rule that gives every flat enough water for the whole day.
constraints: Every flat must get water for drinking, cooking and washing.
The tank fills only once a day.
The rule must be easy to check.
Everyone must be able to understand it.
materials: the results of your Shared Pond Test
general: Limit how much each flat may store, for example drums filled once a day.
Ban uses that waste a lot, such as washing cars with a hose, until the rains.
Choose someone to check the tank level at a fixed time and write it down.
creative: Give each floor a time to fill its drums, so the top floor goes first one day and last the next.
Put a simple marker on the tank, so everyone can see the level from the stairs.
Collect water from the air conditioners or the rain for washing floors.
challenges.your_turn: Now write your own rule for a real shared thing in your building or street. Say who checks it, and what happens if someone breaks it.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Fair Water challenge.

challenges.title: Make a Helper's Work Easier
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You find one small thing your family can do to make a helper's work easier.
challenges.problem: Choose a helper who comes to your home or building, such as the milk delivery person, the garbage collector or the postwoman. Find one thing that slows them down or makes their work harder. Design a change that your family can make in a week.
constraints: The change must cost almost nothing.
Your family must be able to do it.
Ask the helper whether it really helps.
materials: card, string or an old bag, if your design needs one
general: Hang a bag on the door handle for the milk packets.
Keep wet and dry waste in separate bags, tied, at the time the collector comes.
Write your flat number clearly on the door and the letter box.
creative: Put a small bell at the gate with a sign 'Delivery: press here'.
Leave a bottle of cool water for the helpers on hot days.
Make a thank-you card with the names of all your building's helpers.
challenges.your_turn: Now try your change for one week. At the end, ask the helper what difference it made.

quiz.p: Farhan's family eats idli for breakfast. Which of these people's work was needed to make it?
opts: The farmer, the shopkeeper, the gas delivery man and Amma
Only the shopkeeper, who sold the rice
quiz.why: Many people's work is in one plate: the farmer grew the rice and dal, the shopkeeper sold them, the gas delivery man brought the cylinder and Amma cooked. Choosing only one person means seeing only the last step.

quiz.p: Meenakshi says a sweeper's work is less important than a doctor's. What would happen if no sweeper came to her street for a month?
opts: Garbage would pile up, drains would block, and people could fall ill
The doctors would sweep the street
quiz.why: Without sweepers, garbage and blocked drains bring flies, mosquitoes and illness. Then the doctor has more sick people. Both jobs keep the street healthy, so neither is small.

quiz.p: Who pays for the government school, the fire service and the street lights?
opts: Only the people who use them that day
quiz.why: Public services are paid for with taxes, which people and shops pay to the government. Most things you buy include a tax called GST. So they are free to use, but not free to run.

quiz.p: Kavya sees smoke coming from the flat below. Which number should she call?
quiz.why: 112 is India's single emergency number. It brings the fire service, the police or an ambulance. 1098 is the helpline for children who need help.

quiz.p: Which of these is a shared resource?
opts: The water tank on the roof of a building
quiz.why: Many flats use the tank, and the water one flat uses is not there for the others. Arjun's bottle is his alone. A song on the radio is shared, but your listening does not leave less song for anyone.

quiz.p: In the Shared Pond Test, 12 fish are left after a round. The fish left double, but the pond holds at most 20. How many fish are in the pond for the next round?
quiz.why: 12 doubled is 24, but the pond can hold only 20. So the pond has 20 fish. Choosing 24 forgets that a pond has only so much room and food.

quiz.p: Four players share a pond of 20 fish in the Shared Pond Test. Each one takes 5 fish in the first round. What happens?
opts: No fish are left, so the pond is empty for good
quiz.why: 5 fish each for 4 players is 20 fish, the whole pond. No fish are left to double, so no new fish come. Taking everything at once ends the game for everyone.

quiz.p: In Revathi's family, the pond lasted in the talking game but ran out in the silent game. What made the difference?
opts: They talked and agreed a rule before choosing
quiz.why: The fish, the players and the rounds were the same. Only the talking changed, so the talking and the rule made the difference.

quiz.p: What did Elinor Ostrom find when she studied villages that share meadows, forests and water?
opts: Many villages keep shared things for hundreds of years with their own rules
Only governments can look after shared things
quiz.why: Ostrom found that many communities make their own rules, check them and keep their shared things for centuries. In 2009 she became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Economics.

quiz.p: Garrett Hardin wrote in 1968 that shared things are always spoiled. Why did he think so?
opts: Because each person gains the whole fish, but shares the loss with everyone
Because people do not like fish
Because ponds dry up in summer
quiz.why: Hardin said each user gets all the gain from taking more, but the harm is shared by all. So each keeps taking. Ostrom showed this is not always what happens.

quiz.p: The children in Divya's building share one swing. They keep fighting. Which rule is most likely to work?
opts: The children agree turns of 20 pushes each, and one child counts
quiz.why: A rule that the users agree together, with someone checking, is what Ostrom found works best. 'The biggest child decides' is not fair. 'Nobody uses it' wastes the swing.

quiz.p: Which of these did India's Constitution do, under Dr B.R. Ambedkar's lead?
opts: It said each person must do their family's work
It ended untouchability and gave every citizen the right to choose their work
It made all jobs pay the same
quiz.why: The Constitution came into force in 1950. It ended untouchability and gives every citizen the right to choose their profession. It did not make every job pay the same.

items.p: Put the steps of one round of the Shared Pond Test in order.
a: Each player writes a number in secret
Double the fish left, up to 20
items.why: Players choose in secret first, so nobody copies. Then the fish are taken, and the ones left breed.
items: Double the fish left, up to 20
Each player writes a number in secret

items.p: In one round of the Shared Pond Test, Amma takes 3 fish, Paati takes 2, Karthik takes 4 and Revathi takes 1. How many fish did they take in all?
items.why: 3 + 2 + 4 + 1 = 10. A strong answer adds that 10 fish are left from 20, and 10 doubled is 20, so the pond stays full.

items.p: In your Shared Pond Test, which game made the pond last longer? Use your numbers to say why.
items.a: For example: the talking game. We took 10 fish in all each round, so 10 were left and doubled back to 20. In the silent game we took 19, so only 1 was left.
items.why: A strong answer names the game, gives real numbers from the table, and says how many fish were left to double.

items.a: A drawing of a real helper with their tool, their name and their work.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the tool clearly, such as the broom, the iron or the post bag, and uses the helper's real name.

items.p: Divya buys a notebook at a shop. Part of the price is a tax called GST. Where does that tax money go?
items.why: Taxes go to the government, which uses them for public services. That is how a child buying a notebook helps pay for schools and roads.
opts: To the government, to pay for things like roads and schools

items.p: A helper's job is easy, because anyone could do it without learning.
items.why: False. Every job takes skill and practice. Try stringing jasmine as fast as the flower seller, or ironing a shirt as smoothly as the presswala.

items.p: Three of these are public services. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: The post office, the fire service and the government health centre are run for everyone. A private tailoring shop is a business you pay yourself.

items.p: Choose one helper from your list. What would happen to your family if they did not come for a whole week?
items.a: For example: without the garbage collector, our bins would overflow, flies would come, and we might fall ill.
items.why: A strong answer names a real helper and gives at least two things that would go wrong.

items.p: Two children talk about the shared swing in their building's park.
items.a: A strong answer picks one side, gives a reason from the Shared Pond Test, and says one thing the other child has right. For example: Anjali is right that the swing gets broken, but a rule made together, like turns of 20 pushes, may keep it in use for everyone.
items.why: Both have a point. A lock stops overuse but wastes the swing. A rule made together keeps it in use, but only if people keep it.

worksheets.title: Why Shared Things Last or Run Out (stretch)

items.p: Revathi's building has 12 flats. Every flat says, "I only take my share." Yet the tank is empty by afternoon. What is the most likely reason?
items.why: Each flat's share seemed small to them, but all the shares added up to more than the tank holds. This is just what happened in the silent pond game.
opts: Each flat's share added up to more than the tank holds
The water leaked out of the sky

items.p: Garrett Hardin said shared things are always ruined. Elinor Ostrom found villages that kept them for centuries. Write how both could be right about different shared things.
items.a: For example: a small village where people know each other can talk and agree rules, so the meadow lasts. The sea is shared by millions of strangers who cannot all talk, so fish get used up.
items.why: A strong answer gives one example where Ostrom's view fits and one where Hardin's fits, and says what is different between them.

items.p: In a pond game with 3 players, the pond starts with 20 fish. Each player takes 3 fish every round. How many fish are left after the players take their fish?
items.why: 3 players take 3 each, which is 9. 20 take away 9 is 11. A strong answer adds that 11 doubled is 22, so the pond fills back to 20.

items.p: Kavya wants the pond to stay full in the Shared Pond Test. What is the smallest number of fish that must be left after each round?
items.why: 10 fish doubled is 20, so the pond fills up again. 5 doubled is only 10. 20 means nobody takes any fish at all.

items.p: Three people talk about the village pond in Nandini's grandmother's village near Thanjavur.
items.a: A strong answer picks one view, gives a reason, and says what another view has right. For example: the panchayat can make fair rules for the whole village, but the fisherwoman is right that the people who use the pond know it best.
items.why: Each view has truth. Ostrom found that rules made by the users often work best, but a government can help when users cannot agree.

views.who: A fisherwoman who has fished the pond for 30 years
views.says: We fishers should make the rules. We know when the fish breed and which corners they hide in.

views.who: A member of the gram panchayat
views.says: The panchayat should make the rules, because the pond belongs to the whole village, not only the fishers.
We should count the fish every year, and set the limit from the count.

items.ask: Whose idea would you choose? Give a reason. Then say one thing another person has right.

items.p: Match each public service to what it does.
items.why: Each public service does a job too big for one family.
pairs: vaccines and care for the sick

items.p: In the silent pond game, the players could have kept the pond full without talking, if each one had taken only a few fish.
items.why: True. The pond only needs 10 fish left each round. Players could guess this alone, but without talking they cannot be sure others will hold back too.

items.p: Draw a line graph of your Shared Pond Test. Put the rounds along the bottom and the fish in the pond up the side. Draw one line for each game.
items.a: Two lines: the silent game falling to 0, and the talking game staying near 20.
items.why: A strong graph labels both axes and both lines, and the reader can see at a glance which pond lasted.

items.p: Sort these helpers. Is each one usually paid by the family, or by taxes?
items.why: Public services are paid for by taxes. Other helpers are paid by the family that uses them.

items.p: The farmers in Paati's village near Kanchipuram shared one rain tank, called an eri. Who opened the sluice so each field got water in turn?
items.why: The neerkatti was the water keeper of a Tamil Nadu village tank. He opened the sluice for each field in turn, and the farmers paid him with a share of their harvest.
opts: The neerkatti, the village water keeper

items.p: A shared resource, which many people use and nobody owns alone, is also called a ____.
items.why: Scientists call a shared resource a commons.

items.p: Your building's notice board says, 'No car washing with tank water in May.' Explain why the rule is there, and how people would know if someone broke it.
items.a: For example: in May the tank has little water, and a hose uses a lot. The caretaker or the neighbours would see the wet car and the hose.
items.why: A strong answer gives the reason for the rule and a real way to check it, such as a caretaker's notebook.

items.p: Put the steps of the Postcard Test in order.
a: Guess how many days it will take
Write the address and PIN code
Post the card and write the date
Count the days when it arrives
items.why: You guess first, so it is a real prediction. Then you post the card and count the days.
items: Count the days when it arrives
Post the card and write the date
Guess how many days it will take
Write the address and PIN code

items.why: The PIN code is the 6-digit number that leads the card to the right post office.

items.p: Three of these are things a community shares. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: A road, the air and a village pond are used by many people together. A toothbrush belongs to one person.

items.p: In the silent game, everyone took 5 fish and the pond ran out. Nobody was trying to empty it. Write why it still ran out, in your own words.
items.a: Each player only thought about their own fish. Nobody could see what the others would take. Together they took 20, so nothing was left to breed.
items.why: A strong answer says that each choice was small, but all the choices added together were too many.

items.p: Moumita in Kolkata and Shalini in Bengaluru argue about how to keep their city's lake clean.
items.a: A strong answer picks one side with a reason, perhaps from the Shared Pond Test or the Rule Hunt, and says one thing the other side has right. For example: Shalini is right that people who live by the lake can watch it every day, but Moumita is right that a city government can stop a big factory that does not listen.
items.why: Both are real views. Ostrom found that local groups often do well, but they may need help from a government against big polluters.

views.says: The city government should fine anyone who throws waste in the lake. People only listen to fines.
The people who live near the lake should make a group, make rules and take turns to watch it. They care about it most.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say what the other girl has right.

items.p: Arjun plays the pond game with 4 players. They agree 'each takes 2 fish'. Then one player secretly takes 5. The pond starts the round with 20. How many fish are left after the round, before doubling?
items.why: Three players take 2 each, which is 6, and one takes 5. 6 and 5 make 11. 20 take away 11 is 9. Then 9 doubles to 18, so the pond is a little lower. If this happens every round, the pond slowly shrinks.

items.p: Ostrom found that a rule lasts better when someone checks it and breaking it has a small cost. Design a rule for the lift in a 10-floor building at the busy morning hour. Say who checks it and what happens if someone breaks it.
items.a: For example: in the morning, people going down from the top floors go first, and people on floors 1 and 2 take the stairs. The watchman stands by the lift from 8 to 9. The first time someone breaks it, he reminds them. The second time, the residents' meeting talks about it.
items.why: A strong rule says exactly what people do, who checks, and a small cost that grows.

items.p: In the talking game, 4 players each take 2 fish every round for 6 rounds. How many fish does each player catch in all?
items.why: 2 fish a round for 6 rounds is 2 times 6, which is 12. In the silent game, a player who took 5 in the first round may get only 5 or 6 in all.

items.p: Elinor Ostrom showed that shared things never get used up.
items.why: False. She showed that many communities keep shared things for a long time with good rules. Without good rules, shared things are often used up, as Hardin warned.

items.p: In Kerala, the government bans most fishing by big boats in the sea for some weeks each monsoon. Why might this help the fish?
items.why: The ban falls in the season when many fish breed. Leaving the fish alone then lets more young fish grow, like leaving fish in the pond to double.
opts: Many fish breed in those weeks, so more young fish grow

items.p: Sort these changes. Would each one help a shared tank last longer, or make it run out faster?
items.why: Anything that limits use, or lets people check use, helps a shared thing last.
items: a caretaker writes the tank level every afternoon
each flat fills as many drums as it wants
no car washing with tank water in summer
nobody knows who is using the water
the residents agree the rules at a meeting
a tap left dripping in the lobby

items.p: Draw your building or street as a pond. Draw the shared things in it, such as the tank, the lift and the park, and the people who use them. Add one rule for each.
items.a: A drawing of the building with its shared things, the people who use them and one rule for each.
items.why: A strong drawing shows at least three shared things, with a rule that says who may use each and how much.

items.p: Many people think a job is 'small' if it is done with the hands. Use your helper interview to argue against this.
items.a: For example: the presswala told me he learned for years, and his iron is heavy and hot. If he did not come, our clothes would not be ready for school.
items.why: A strong answer uses something the helper really said, names the skill the job needs, and says who depends on it.

items.p: Three of these helped a shared thing last in the stories and tests of this unit. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Agreeing a rule, a water keeper and a caretaker's notebook all helped. Choosing in silence is what made the pond run out.
opts: The neerkatti opening the sluice in turn
Selvi akka's notebook of the tank level

items.p: Here is a picture of an old village tank in Tamil Nadu. Label the parts: the tank, the bank, the sluice, the fields.
a: A: the tank, which stores rain
B: the bank, which holds the water in
C: the sluice, the gate that lets water out
D: the fields that get the water
items.why: The tank stores the monsoon rain. The sluice lets out water a little at a time, so the fields get water in turn.

items.p: In 2009, ____ became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Economics, for her work on how people share things.
items.why: Elinor Ostrom studied shared meadows, forests and water around the world.

items.p: Gauri in Pune says, "Public services are free." What is the best answer to her?
items.why: Using them is free or cheap, but they cost money to run. That money comes from taxes, which almost everyone pays, for example through GST on things they buy.
opts: She is right, they cost nothing
Only rich people pay for them
They are free to use, but everyone pays for them through taxes

items.p: Revathi's family talked before the second pond game. What else, besides talking, helped the pond last? Use the story or your own test.
items.a: For example: Paati counted the bowl after every round, so everyone could see whether the rule was kept. Everyone also knew the number to leave, which was 10.
items.why: A strong answer names something more than talk: a clear limit, a person who checks, or a way to see the pond.

applications: Residents' associations in apartment blocks use water rules, tank records and meeting votes to share water in summer.
Fishing communities and governments agree seasons with no fishing, so fish can breed. Kerala and other coastal states have a monsoon ban on most trawling.
Village tank groups in Tamil Nadu have restored old eris with the help of groups such as the DHAN Foundation, bringing back water-sharing rules.
Cities plan where to put schools, health centres and fire stations so that every family can reach one.
Scientists use pond games like the Shared Pond Test to study how people share, in villages and in laboratories.

open_questions.q: How can millions of people who never meet share the air and the sea?
open_questions.why_open: Small groups who can talk often share well. Nobody has found a way that works as well for the whole world. Scientists and countries are still arguing about it.

open_questions.q: Why do some people keep a rule when nobody is watching?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists say it is trust, some say it is habit or wanting to be seen as fair. Studies find all of these matter, but not how much each one does.

open_questions.q: Which jobs will people still do in fifty years?
open_questions.why_open: Machines already do some work people once did, and new jobs keep appearing. Nobody can say for sure which jobs will stay.

maths.problem: In the Shared Pond Test, the pond holds at most 20 fish. Fill in what the pond will have after doubling, if 4, 7, 10 and 13 fish are left.
maths.answer: 4 becomes 8. 7 becomes 14. 10 becomes 20. 13 would be 26, but the pond holds only 20, so it becomes 20.
maths.explain: Doubling means adding a number to itself: 4 and 4 make 8, 7 and 7 make 14, 10 and 10 make 20. 13 and 13 make 26, which is more than 20, so the pond stops at 20. So any number from 10 up refills the pond.
maths.context: This is about the Shared Pond Test, where the fish left in the pond double each round.
maths.why_maths: Doubling shows the rule hidden in the game: leave at least 10 fish and the pond fills up again.

maths.problem: In the silent game, 4 players caught these fish in all: Amma 6, Paati 5, Karthik 6 and Revathi 5. In the talking game, each caught 12. How many more fish did the family catch in all in the talking game?
maths.answer: 26 more fish. The silent game gave 22 fish, and the talking game gave 48.
maths.explain: Silent game: 6 + 5 + 6 + 5 = 22. Talking game: 4 players times 12 is 48. 48 take away 22 is 26. So holding back each round gave everyone more in the end.
maths.context: This is about the Shared Pond Test, played once in silence and once after agreeing a rule.
maths.why_maths: Adding up both games shows that taking less each round can mean catching more in all.

maths.problem: A building's tank holds 6,000 litres. 12 flats share it. If each flat uses the same amount, how much water can each flat use in a day?
maths.explain: Share 6,000 litres into 12 equal parts. 12 times 500 is 6,000, so each flat gets 500 litres. If one flat uses 1,000 litres, another flat gets only what is left.
maths.context: This is about sharing one water tank between the flats of a building, like the tank in the story The Tank on the Roof.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the tank fairly tells each flat what its share is, so everyone can see when someone takes more.

maths.problem: Revathi posts a postcard on the 3rd of the month. It arrives on the 7th. Her cousin's card to a far town arrives on the 10th. How many more days did the far card take?
maths.answer: 3 more days. Revathi's card took 4 days, and the far card took 7.
maths.explain: From the 3rd to the 7th is 4 days. From the 3rd to the 10th is 7 days. 7 take away 4 is 3. The far card travelled further and went through more sorting offices.
maths.context: This is about the Postcard Test, where you count the days a card takes to arrive.
maths.why_maths: Counting days on a calendar turns two dates into a time you can compare between cards.

maths.problem: A family pays the presswala 10 rupees for each shirt. They send 7 shirts a week. How much do they pay in 4 weeks?
maths.explain: 7 shirts at 10 rupees is 70 rupees a week. 4 weeks of 70 rupees is 280 rupees. This money is the presswala's livelihood: what he earns to live.
maths.context: This is about the presswala you may have met in Meet a Helper, who earns his living by ironing clothes.
maths.why_maths: Working out a helper's earnings shows how their work turns into the money their family lives on.
