roots.context: We have met the helpers who keep our neighbourhood going, and tested a shared pond in silence and after talking. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the silent game, each player took a lot, and the pond was empty within a few rounds. In the talking game, you agreed a rule, and the pond stayed full to the end. Each player also caught more fish in all. So a shared thing can last when the people who use it make rules together.
deep_truth.habit: We split things into 'mine' and 'nobody's'. We look after what is ours, and think a shared thing is nobody's job, so it is bound to be spoiled. The pond showed a third kind: a thing that is ours together, and lasts when we act together.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Shared Pond Test, the pond ran out quickly when players chose in silence, and lasted when they talked and agreed a limit first. Ostrom's studies found village meadows, water channels and forests kept for centuries in the same way.

three.who_am_i: You are one of many people who use the same water, roads and air. What you take, and what you leave, reaches all of them.
three.what_is_life: Life in a community is always shared: the work of many hands, and the things that many people use.
three.what_is_this_world: It is a world where the same tank can run dry or last, depending on what the people around it agree.

roots.thread: A pond is one body of water, but many families drink from it. Each family is separate, with its own bucket and its own wants. When they talk and agree, the many families begin to act like one, and the one pond can feed them all. The fish in the pond, the families around it and the rule they made are one living whole. A community is many people learning to act as one.

teachings.teaching: The wealth of a wise person who loves the world is like the village tank, the ooruni, full of water: everyone can drink from it.
teachings.link: Valluvar picked the shared village tank as his picture of good wealth. A full tank is good because it is open to everyone, which only lasts if everyone takes care of it.

teachings.teaching: Come together, speak together, let your minds agree.
teachings.link: In the Shared Pond Test, the only change between the two games was speaking together. That was enough to keep the pond full.

teachings.teaching: To share your food and protect many lives is the first of all the good things the wise have taught.
teachings.link: Keeping fish in the pond for others is a kind of sharing food. It protects the families and the fish too.

science.text: Groups who can talk with each other take less from a shared pool, and keep it longer, than groups who cannot talk.
How to protect very large shared things, such as the fish in the sea or the air of the whole Earth, is still argued about.

other_view.who: Garrett Hardin, in The Tragedy of the Commons (1968), and people who agree with him today
other_view.view: Talking is not enough when millions of strangers share something, like the sea or the sky. Each one gains from cheating a little. So we need laws, owners or governments with the power to stop people, not only promises.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat. The Shared Pond Test needs only chana, a steel bowl and paper slips, and three or four players from the family. The numbers were checked: with 4 players taking up to 5 each, greedy play takes 20 of 20 fish and ends the pond at once, while leaving 10 refills it to 20 every round. The limit changes with the number of players (8 for 2 players, 3 for 5 or more), so greedy play still empties the pond and a rule can still save it. Grown-ups are told to play for themselves in both games, so the result is not steered, and a pond that survives the silent game is treated as a real result. The Postcard Test needs one postcard and a relative in another town, with a grown-up at the post box. The interview, the water trail and the rule hunt are marked for a grown-up. The corridor plant can be shared within the family if there are no neighbours' children. The spine is the intro, Who Keeps Our Building Going, the Shared Pond Test, the explanation cards, roots and the quiz, about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1968, the American ecologist Garrett Hardin wrote an essay called The Tragedy of the Commons. He pictured herders sharing one field. Each herder gains a whole cow by adding one more, but the harm to the grass is shared by all. So, he wrote, each herder keeps adding cows until the field is ruined. Many people took this as a law: shared things are always spoiled, unless a government or an owner takes control. Elinor Ostrom, a political scientist at Indiana University, wanted to see what really happened. With her team, she studied real places: mountain meadows shared by Swiss villages for centuries, water channels in Spain and Nepal, forests and fishing grounds. Many had lasted for hundreds of years, kept by rules the users made themselves. In laboratory games, she and her colleagues found that people allowed to talk took far less from a shared pool. Her book Governing the Commons came out in 1990. In 2009 she became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Economics.
how_we_found_out.who: Garrett Hardin, and Elinor Ostrom of Indiana University with her colleagues, including Roy Gardner and James Walker
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought shared things are always ruined, because each user takes too much, unless a government or an owner controls them. Ostrom found many communities that kept shared meadows, water and forests for centuries with their own rules.
